passages.text: Digital cameras capture images by turning light into electrical signals, then processing those signals into digital files. Understanding how do digital cameras capture images makes photography much easier. A digital camera is a small, precise system that guides light through a lens, measures it with a sensor, and builds a picture from millions of tiny data points. This guide explains each stage in clear terms, from pressing the shutter to saving a JPEG or RAW file. The Basic Process: From Light to Image The simplest answer to how do digital cameras capture images is that they convert light into data. The camera does not record a scene in one instant as a complete picture. Instead, it measures the light reaching its image sensor at thousands or millions of individual points. Here is the process in order: - Light reflects from a subject and enters the camera. - The lens focuses that light onto the image sensor. - The sensor converts light into electrical signals. - The camera measures and interprets those signals. - The image processor turns the data into a photograph. - The camera saves the result to a memory card or internal storage. This process happens very quickly.

The Role of the Camera Lens The camera lens is perhaps the most important component in image formation. Its primary function is to focus light rays onto the image sensor (in digital cameras) or film (in analog cameras). When light reflects off an object, it scatters in all directions. A lens gathers and focuses these scattered light rays into a single coherent point to create a sharp image. Lenses work based on the principle of refraction—the bending of light when it passes from one medium to another, such as air to glass. The most common pattern is the Bayer filter. It places red, green, and blue filters over different photosites, with extra green filters because human vision is highly sensitive to green detail. The camera then estimates missing color information by comparing nearby photosites. This process is called demosaicing. Dynamic Range Dynamic range is the span between the darkest and brightest detail a sensor can record. A camera with wide dynamic range may preserve texture in both a bright sky and a shaded building. If highlights receive too much light, they become clipped and turn pure white. If shadows receive too little light, they may become solid black. Once detail is clipped, editing software usually cannot fully restore it. This is why photographers often protect bright highlights, especially in scenes with strong sunlight. RAW files may preserve more recoverable information than JPEG files, but they cannot recover detail that the sensor never recorded.
